summary: This sample is the Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) low-density steel designated "19Al" in the paper by Wang et al., in its terminal state after solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min (argon, oil quenched) followed by aging at 650 °C for 3 h and water quenching. The study asks how the Al content (15, 17, 19 at.%) controls the aging hardening behaviour of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels, in which ultra-high hardness is produced by the precipitation of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase. At 650 °C, i.e. well above 600 °C, the α (BCC) matrix of the 19Al alloy is almost completely transformed into β-Mn within the first hour of aging, and this 3 h condition accordingly consists of a β-Mn matrix carrying fine new BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates at the β-Mn interfaces, with a Vickers hardness of 801.5 ± 20.3 HV.
composition: Nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%). The alloy was melted from high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials; the chemical composition measured by EDS is Fe 41.6, Mn 34.8, Al 18.6 and Cu 5.0 at.% (Table 1), so the nominal Al variation across the 15Al/17Al/19Al series is achieved essentially by substituting Al for Fe while Mn (~35 at.%) and Cu (5 at.%) are held constant. Iron is the base element; a high Mn content of about 35 at.% was deliberately chosen to promote the precipitation kinetics of the hard β-Mn phase responsible for the ultra-high and flexible hardness; Al is the primary density-reducing element (1 wt.% Al lowers the density by roughly 0.1 g·cm⁻³) and also stabilizes the Al-rich D0₃ phase; Cu was added because it both accelerates the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn and enhances the hardness of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steel. The measured density of this 19Al alloy is 6.66 g·cm⁻³ (15Al: 6.85 g·cm⁻³; 17Al: 6.76 g·cm⁻³).
processing: Processing lineage: (1) vacuum induction melting of high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials under an argon atmosphere to produce Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) ingots; (2) homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 h; (3) hot rolling into plates 4 mm thick; (4) electrical discharge machining of the plates into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimens for Vickers hardness measurement and microstructural characterization; (5) solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon followed by oil quenching, which yields a single-phase α (BCC) matrix; (6) final aging at 650 °C for 3 h followed by water quenching, the terminal state of this sample. Electrolytic polishing in a 10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol mixture was used to prepare hardness/XRD/SEM/EBSD specimens.
microstructure: The solution-treated state of the 19Al alloy is a single-phase α (BCC) matrix; among the three alloys the 19Al solution-treated condition showed the finest, equiaxed multi-coloured grain structure in EBSD inverse pole figures. In this 650 °C / 3 h aged condition the α matrix has almost completely transformed into β-Mn, consistent with the paper's general finding that at 600 °C and above the α→β-Mn transformation in the 19Al (and 17Al) alloy is nearly complete after only 1 h of aging. Fine precipitates of a new BCC phase and of an FCC Cu-rich phase form at/within the interfaces between the β-Mn grains. The reported phase evolution sequence is α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase, i.e. the Mn-rich α-Mn and β-Mn co-precipitate before the α matrix is fully consumed and the late BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases appear once β-Mn dominates. In the β-Mn of the hardest 19Al sample the β-Mn was found to be Mn-rich and poor in Al and Cu (SEM-EDS: 36.2 at.% Mn, 17.5 at.% Al, 2.6 at.% Cu), and the FCC Cu-rich precipitates were Cu-rich, depleted in Fe and Mn and slightly poor in Al, frequently containing FCC twins. Note that no EBSD, SEM, XRD or TEM characterization is reported specifically for the 19Al 650 °C / 3 h condition; the closest 19Al datasets are EBSD at 525 °C/10 h, 600 °C/3 h and 650 °C/6 h, SE images over the whole aging matrix, and XRD at 550 °C/6 h.
properties: Mechanical: Vickers hardness of this 19Al 650 °C / 3 h sample is 801.5 ± 20.3 HV (load 9.8 N, dwell 15 s, 5 measurements averaged on a 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimen, HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester). No tensile, fatigue, creep or fracture-toughness values are reported for this specific condition. Physical: density 6.66 g·cm⁻³ (Archimedes method, alloy-level value). Across all of its aging conditions the 19Al alloy spans 263.8 HV (solution-treated) to 917.8 HV, with the peak reached at 600 °C/10 h, and the optimal aging window for ultra-high hardness of the 19Al alloy is 575–625 °C. Characterization techniques applied in the study as a whole (not all to this condition) are Vickers hardness testing, nanoindentation (Agilent G200, 200 nm depth), XRD (D8 Discover), SE imaging and EDS (ZEISS Sigma 300, 5 kV), EBSD (GeminiSEM 300, step 1.5 µm low-magnification / 0.05 µm high-magnification) and TEM/HRTEM with EDS (FEI Talos F200X, 200 kV).
mechanisms: Aging above ~600 °C drives the α (BCC) matrix almost completely to β-Mn within about 1 h, so by 3 h at 650 °C the 19Al alloy is essentially a β-Mn matrix; the acceleration is attributed to an increased driving force for β-Mn formation together with a faster atomic diffusion rate at higher temperature.

Because β-Mn has a very high intrinsic hardness (>10 GPa, nanoindentation), the massive formation of β-Mn during aging is the origin of the ultra-high hardness of the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels; even the 650 °C / 3 h condition reaches ~800 HV.

β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase whose nucleation and growth require long-range diffusion, enriching Mn and expelling Fe, Al and Cu into the surrounding matrix; the Al enriched at the β-Mn interfaces stabilizes the new BCC phase that forms there, while the limited solubility of Cu in Fe-based alloys causes the expelled Cu to form the FCC Cu-rich phase at the same interfaces.

Increasing the Al content slows the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn: the extra Al atoms enriched around the growing β-Mn particles hinder their further growth, and the Al-stabilized D0₃ phase (larger in amount and size at higher Al) must first be depleted before β-Mn can nucleate and grow.

The hardness of the ultra-hard alloys depends both on the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn and on the absolute volume fraction of β-Mn: higher Al raises the Al dissolved in β-Mn (14.3 → 16.3 → 17.5 at.% for 15Al → 17Al → 19Al), giving a marginal solid-solution strengthening of β-Mn, but it also increases the amount of softer FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates at the β-Mn interfaces, lowering the absolute β-Mn fraction and hence the overall hardness (e.g. volume fraction of these precipitates 3.9 % at 15Al 650 °C/3 h vs 6.5 % at 19Al 650 °C/6 h).

Fracture toughness falls with increasing Al because (i) the intrinsically harder β-Mn embrittles the alloy and (ii) the ductile FCC Cu-rich phase at the β-Mn interfaces decreases as Al increases, so the toughening contribution of the FCC phase is progressively lost.

Solution-treated hardness increases with Al content through solid-solution strengthening, whereas the aged-peak hardness decreases with Al content; the two effects arise from the opposing roles of Al in the α matrix (solute strengthening) and in the aged β-Mn + precipitate architecture (dilution of β-Mn).
conclusions: This 19Al sample ageing at 650 °C for 3 h delivers 801.5 ± 20.3 HV, a value well above the solution-treated baseline of 263.8 HV and representative of the high-temperature, near-plateau branch of the 19Al ageing response: at 625 °C and 650 °C the 19Al hardness is essentially time-independent at about 855–871 HV and 801–811 HV respectively, whereas the alloy's maximum of 917.8 HV is reached at 600 °C/10 h. The work establishes that Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels can be aged over 525–650 °C for ≤10 h to give an ultra-wide, tunable hardness window of 253.4–965.6 HV driven by continuous β-Mn precipitation, with the 15Al composition reaching an ultra-high specific hardness of 141 HV·cm³/g (965.6 HV at 6.66–6.85 g·cm⁻³ density class) — the highest among the low-density steels, conventional steels, pure iron and M/HEAs compared in the Ashby plot. Increasing Al content, however, slows the β-Mn precipitation kinetics (complete α→β-Mn needs 3 h at 525 °C for 15Al but 6 h at 550 °C for 17Al and 10 h at 550 °C for 19Al), slightly increases the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn, and simultaneously decreases the FCC Cu-rich phase at the β-Mn interfaces and the fracture toughness of the ultra-hard alloys, thereby lowering the final hardening effect. Practically, these alloys can be shaped in the soft solution-treated state and then short-time aged to the required hardness, offering a "one material, multiple uses" route for lightweight structural and wear-resistant components; the still-insufficient toughness of the hardest states is identified as an open problem.
unmapped: The elastic modulus (181 GPa, from compressive stress-strain curves) and fracture toughness KIC (3.5 MPa·m^1/2, from an average crack length of 35 µm) reported for 19Al correspond to the hardest 19Al sample (peak hardness 917.8 HV at 600 °C/10 h), not to this 650 °C/3 h condition.

The 19Al β-Mn intrinsic hardness determined by nanoindentation (12.5 ± 0.4 GPa) and the β-Mn Al content (17.5 at.% by SEM-EDS) were measured on the hardest 19Al sample, not on this 650 °C/3 h condition.
The ultra-high specific hardness of 141 HV·cm³/g and the highest specific-hardness value among the authors' alloys belong to the Fe-35.2Mn-15.2Al-5.2Cu (15Al) alloy, not to the 19Al alloy.
The volume fraction of FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates for the 19Al alloy (6.5 %, hardness 810.9 HV) corresponds to aging at 650 °C for 6 h, not to this 650 °C/3 h condition.

TEM analysis was performed only on 15Al 600 °C/6 h and 17Al 575 °C/6 h; no TEM, EBSD, SEM or XRD data are reported specifically for the 19Al 650 °C/3 h sample, so its phase constitution is inferred from the alloy-level aging sequence rather than measured directly on this specimen.
